reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Encompasses a spectrum from ineffective oesophageal motility, defined on high-resolution manometry by a high proportion of weak or failed swallows, to absent contractility where no effective peristalsis is present with normal sphincter relaxation.
Strongly associated with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease because poor peristaltic clearance prolongs acid contact time and predisposes to severe reflux and its complications.
Absent contractility with a poorly relaxing sphincter should prompt evaluation for achalasia; when relaxation is normal it may reflect an end-stage or scleroderma-type pattern.

Systemic sclerosis characteristically produces a hypomotile smooth-muscle oesophagus with a patulous, hypotensive lower sphincter, and oesophageal involvement is often an early feature of the disease.
Symptoms include dysphagia (often to solids and worse when supine), heartburn and regurgitation; some patients are asymptomatic despite marked manometric abnormality.
Management centres on aggressive acid suppression and reflux precautions rather than prokinetics, as available prokinetic agents have limited efficacy on the aperistaltic oesophagus.
Anti-reflux surgery must be approached with caution because a partial (rather than complete) fundoplication is usually preferred to avoid precipitating dysphagia in a poorly clearing oesophagus.
Screen for an underlying connective-tissue disease, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism or a myopathic/neuropathic process when hypomotility is severe or of recent onset.
reference.pathophysiology: Oesophageal hypomotility results from failure of the smooth-muscle segment to generate contractions of adequate vigour and coordination to clear a bolus. The defect may lie in the myenteric neurons, in cholinergic excitatory signalling, or in the smooth muscle itself. In systemic sclerosis, progressive smooth-muscle atrophy and fibrosis of the distal two-thirds of the oesophagus, together with incompetence of the lower oesophageal sphincter, produce weak or absent peristalsis and severe reflux. Diabetic autonomic neuropathy, hypothyroidism, amyloidosis and certain medications can produce similar hypocontractility. The common physiological consequence is impaired bolus transit and defective acid clearance, which drives reflux disease and, when severe, oesophageal retention and dysphagia.
additionalDifferentials: achalasia (particularly when sphincter relaxation is impaired)
systemic sclerosis and other connective-tissue disease oesophagopathy
gastro-oesophageal reflux disease with secondary peristaltic dysfunction
diabetic or other autonomic neuropathy affecting the oesophagus
oesophageal involvement by amyloidosis or a myopathic process
additionalInvestigations: high-resolution oesophageal manometry with bolus-transit or impedance assessment
upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsies to exclude mucosal disease and eosinophilic oesophagitis
ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring to quantify reflux burden
timed barium oesophagram assessing clearance and emptying
connective-tissue disease serology (antinuclear and scleroderma-associated antibodies)
thyroid function tests and glycaemic assessment
gastric emptying study when a diffuse gut dysmotility is suspected
redFlags: progressive dysphagia with weight loss suggesting stricture, malignancy or evolving achalasia
features of systemic sclerosis such as Raynaud phenomenon, skin tightening or telangiectasia
recurrent aspiration or nocturnal respiratory symptoms from reflux and retention
severe erosive oesophagitis, ulceration or peptic stricture on endoscopy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the underlying cause: idiopathic ineffective motility is often stable and managed by reflux control, whereas the hypomotility of systemic sclerosis tends to be progressive and predisposes to severe reflux disease, stricture and Barrett's oesophagus. Absent contractility is generally irreversible, so treatment aims to control reflux and preserve nutrition rather than restore peristalsis.
pitfalls: Relying on prokinetic drugs, which rarely restore effective peristalsis in a severely hypomotile oesophagus.
Performing a complete (360-degree) fundoplication in a poorly clearing oesophagus and thereby causing intractable dysphagia.
Missing an underlying connective-tissue disease, especially systemic sclerosis, in a patient presenting with reflux and dysphagia.
Failing to distinguish absent contractility with impaired sphincter relaxation (achalasia) from that with normal relaxation.
Underestimating reflux burden and its complications because peristaltic failure prolongs acid exposure.

management: Aggressive acid suppression with proton pump inhibitors as the mainstay, since impaired peristaltic clearance prolongs acid contact time
Reflux precautions: weight loss, head-of-bed elevation, avoiding late or large meals and reflux-provoking foods, and remaining upright after eating
Dysphagia measures such as eating upright, thorough chewing and taking fluids with meals; prokinetic agents have limited benefit in the aperistaltic oesophagus
Treat the underlying cause — systemic sclerosis, hypothyroidism or diabetic autonomic neuropathy — and review medications that impair motility
Evaluate absent contractility with a poorly relaxing sphincter for achalasia before attributing symptoms to hypomotility
Surveillance for reflux complications, with endoscopic dilatation for stricture and monitoring for Barrett's oesophagus
Multidisciplinary gastroenterology and rheumatology care, with caution over anti-reflux surgery given the risk of worsening dysphagia in aperistalsis
